title: '5' + 5 Crashes Python: How Type Conversion Fixes It
excerpt: Fix TypeError surprises by converting values between int, float, str and bool with the right built-in function.

headings.text: Two Values That Look Alike but Are Not
The Safe Case Python Converts for You
Why Comparing Text With Numbers Goes Wrong

html:
To you, 5 and "5" look almost identical. To Python they are different kinds of values, called types, and they behave differently: one is a number you can calculate with, the other is text made of the character "5".

Type conversion means turning a value of one type into another, using functions like int() (whole number), float() (decimal number), str() (text) and bool() (the yes/no values True and False). Python rarely does it for you, so knowing when to convert is what separates a working program from a TypeError, the error Python raises when you use a value of the wrong kind.

Two Values That Look Alike but Are Not

Compare what + does with text and with numbers:

text_five = "5"
number_five = 5

print(text_five + text_five)
print(number_five + number_five)
print(type(text_five), type(number_five))
55
10
<class 'str'> <class 'int'>

With text, + joins the characters, giving 55. With numbers it adds, giving 10. The function type() reports each value's type: str is text and int is a whole number. Now mix them:

print(text_five + number_five)
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

Why doesn't Python simply figure out what you meant? Because there are two reasonable answers, 10 and "55", and guessing wrong would hide a bug. So Python stops and asks you to decide. ("Concatenate" in the message just means joining pieces of text.)

int(), float() and str()

You make the decision by converting one side:

print(int("5") + 5)
print(text_five + str(5))
print(float("3.5") + 1)
10
55
4.5
  • int(x) makes a whole number.
  • float(x) makes a number with a decimal point.
  • str(x) makes text.

Does int() round a decimal number? It does not; it simply cuts off everything after the decimal point:

print(int(3.9))
print(int(-3.9))
print(round(3.9))
3
-3
4

If you want rounding to the nearest whole number, use round(). Notice that int(-3.9) gives -3: int() just drops the decimal part, so 3.9 becomes 3 and -3.9 becomes -3.

bool(): Is There Something Here?

True and False are Python's two yes/no values. bool() turns any value into one of them: zero and empty things (such as "", text with no characters) become False, and everything else becomes True:

print(bool(0))
print(bool(1))
print(bool(""))
print(bool("hello"))
print(bool("False"))
False
True
False
True
True

The last line surprises people: why is bool("False") true? Because "False" is a string with characters in it, and any non-empty string counts as True. bool() checks whether something is empty, not what the text says.

When a Conversion Fails

A conversion only works when the value can really be read as the new type. Isn't "3.5" a number? It is, but not a whole number, so int() refuses it. Python reports this as a ValueError, meaning the value is the right kind of thing but unacceptable for this job:

int("3.5")
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '3.5'

This fails because "3.5" is not a whole number. When you have text that holds a decimal, convert it in two steps, text to float to int:

print(int(float("3.5")))
3

The Safe Case Python Converts for You

If Python rarely converts anything, how does 3 + 2.5 work? Mixing a whole number with a decimal number is a safe case, because no information is lost, so Python gives a decimal number.

total = 3 + 2.5
print(total)
print(type(total))
5.5
<class 'float'>

Why Comparing Text With Numbers Goes Wrong

Types also matter when you compare values. The operator == asks "are these equal?" and < asks "is the left one smaller?"; both answer True or False. The text "10" and the number 10 are never equal, and text is compared character by character, not by size:

print("10" == 10)
print("10" < "9")
print(int("10") < int("9"))
False
True
False

How can "10" < "9" be true? Text is compared one character at a time, like words in a dictionary: the first character "1" comes before "9", so "10" counts as smaller. Convert both sides to numbers first and you get the answer you expect.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonTypeConversion.ipynb.

Summary

  • Python does not guess between text and numbers; mixing "5" and 5 raises a TypeError.
  • int(), float() and str() convert a value to a whole number, a decimal number and text.
  • int() cuts off decimals toward zero; use round() to round.
  • bool() is False for zero and empty values and True for the rest, including the text "False".
  • Converting text that does not look like the target type raises a ValueError.
  • Whole number plus decimal number is a safe mix that Python handles automatically.
